questions.question: An Atwood machine has mass $m_1 = 3\ \mathrm{kg}$ on one side and $m_2 = 5\ \mathrm{kg}$ on the other, connected by a light string over a frictionless, massless pulley. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find: (a) the acceleration of the system, (b) the tension in the string.
questions.answer:
**(a)** Treat the heavier side as driving the motion. Net driving force = $(m_2 - m_1)g$; total inertia = $m_1 + m_2$.

$$a = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{(5-3) \times 10}{3 + 5} = \frac{20}{8} = 2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

**(b)** Apply Newton's second law to $m_1$ (accelerating upward):

$T - m_1 g = m_1 a \Rightarrow T = m_1(g + a) = 3(10 + 2.5) = 37.5\ \mathrm{N}$

Verification on $m_2$: $m_2 g - T = m_2 a \Rightarrow 50 - 37.5 = 12.5 = 5 \times 2.5$ ✓

questions.question: In an Atwood machine with $m_1 = 2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2 = 6\ \mathrm{kg}$, the system starts from rest. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find: (a) the acceleration, (b) the speed of the masses after $m_2$ has descended $1.6\ \mathrm{m}$, (c) the time to reach that speed.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $a = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{4 \times 10}{8} = 5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

**(b)** Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (from rest, $u = 0$):

$v = \sqrt{2 \times 5 \times 1.6} = \sqrt{16} = 4\ \mathrm{m/s}$

**(c)** $v = at \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{v}{a} = \dfrac{4}{5} = 0.8\ \mathrm{s}$

questions.question: One mass $m_1 = 4\ \mathrm{kg}$ is on a **frictionless** incline at $30°$, connected by a string over a frictionless pulley to mass $m_2 = 3\ \mathrm{kg}$ hanging vertically. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find: (a) which way the system moves, (b) the acceleration, (c) the tension.
questions.answer:
Component of $m_1$'s weight along incline (down-slope): $m_1 g\sin 30° = 4 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 20\ \mathrm{N}$

Weight of $m_2$: $m_2 g = 30\ \mathrm{N}$

Since $30 > 20$, **$m_2$ descends and $m_1$ moves up the incline**.

**(b)** Net force = $m_2 g - m_1 g\sin 30°= 30 - 20 = 10\ \mathrm{N}$

$a = \dfrac{10}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{10}{7} \approx 1.43\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

**(c)** From $m_2$: $T = m_2(g - a) = 3\!\left(10 - \dfrac{10}{7}\right) = 3 \times \dfrac{60}{7} = \dfrac{180}{7} \approx 25.7\ \mathrm{N}$

questions.question: In an Atwood machine with $m_1$ and $m_2 > m_1$, the acceleration is $a = g/5$. Find the ratio $m_2/m_1$.

An Atwood machine has $m_1 = 1\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2 = 2\ \mathrm{kg}$. The system is released from rest. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find: (a) the acceleration, (b) the distance each mass moves in the first $3\ \mathrm{s}$, (c) the kinetic energy of the system at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $a = \dfrac{(2-1) \times 10}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{10}{3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \approx 3.33\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

**(b)** $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{10}{3} \times 9 = 15\ \mathrm{m}$

**(c)** Speed at $t = 3\ \mathrm{s}$: $v = at = \dfrac{10}{3} \times 3 = 10\ \mathrm{m/s}$

$KE = \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 100 = 150\ \mathrm{J}$

Verification via work-energy: Work by gravity on $m_2$: $m_2 g s = 2 \times 10 \times 15 = 300\ \mathrm{J}$. Work against gravity on $m_1$: $-m_1 g s = -150\ \mathrm{J}$. Net work $= 150\ \mathrm{J}$ ✓

questions.question: An Atwood machine has $m_1$ and $m_2$. Both masses are at the same height when the system is released. Derive the speed of the masses when $m_2$ has descended a distance $d$, using (a) kinematics and (b) energy conservation. Show both give the same result.
questions.answer:
**(a) Kinematics:**

$a = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}$

$v^2 = 2ad = \dfrac{2(m_2 - m_1)gd}{m_1 + m_2}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(m_2 - m_1)gd}{m_1 + m_2}}$

**(b) Energy conservation:**

$m_2$ descends $d$ (loses PE), $m_1$ ascends $d$ (gains PE); string inextensible so both have speed $v$.

$m_2 gd - m_1 gd = \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)v^2$

$(m_2 - m_1)gd = \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)v^2$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(m_2 - m_1)gd}{m_1 + m_2}}$ ✓ Same result.

questions.question: An Atwood machine has $m_1 = 500\ \mathrm{g}$ and $m_2 = 700\ \mathrm{g}$. The support holding the pulley is a spring scale. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. What does the spring scale read while the masses are in motion?
questions.answer:
The scale supports **two tension forces** (one on each side of the string).

$a = \dfrac{(0.7 - 0.5) \times 10}{0.7 + 0.5} = \dfrac{2}{1.2} = \dfrac{5}{3}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

Tension: $T = m_1(g + a) = 0.5\!\left(10 + \dfrac{5}{3}\right) = 0.5 \times \dfrac{35}{3} = \dfrac{35}{6}\ \mathrm{N}$

The scale reads the total upward force supporting the pulley:

$F_{\text{scale}} = 2T = \dfrac{35}{3} \approx 11.7\ \mathrm{N}$

Note: if the system were static, $F_{\text{scale}} = (m_1 + m_2)g = 12\ \mathrm{N}$ — the reading **decreases** when the masses accelerate.

questions.question: A block of mass $m_1 = 5\ \mathrm{kg}$ is on a rough horizontal table (coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.3$). It is connected by a string over a pulley at the table edge to a hanging mass $m_2 = 4\ \mathrm{kg}$. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find: (a) the acceleration, (b) the tension.
questions.answer:
Friction on $m_1$ (opposing motion, directed away from pulley): $f = \mu_k m_1 g = 0.3 \times 5 \times 10 = 15\ \mathrm{N}$

**(a)** Net driving force $= m_2 g - f = 40 - 15 = 25\ \mathrm{N}$

$a = \dfrac{25}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{25}{9} \approx 2.78\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

**(b)** From hanging mass: $T = m_2(g - a) = 4\!\left(10 - \dfrac{25}{9}\right) = 4 \times \dfrac{65}{9} = \dfrac{260}{9} \approx 28.9\ \mathrm{N}$

questions.question: In an Atwood machine, $m_2 = 3m_1$. The system is released from rest and $m_2$ falls a distance $H$ before hitting the floor. After that, $m_1$ continues upward. How much higher does $m_1$ rise after $m_2$ hits the floor? (Neglect string length complications; assume string goes slack immediately.)
questions.answer:
$a = \dfrac{(3m_1 - m_1)g}{3m_1 + m_1} = \dfrac{2m_1 g}{4m_1} = \dfrac{g}{2}$

Speed of masses just before $m_2$ hits floor:

$v^2 = 2aH = 2 \times \dfrac{g}{2} \times H = gH \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{gH}$

After impact, $m_1$ continues upward with initial speed $v$ and decelerates under gravity:

$\Delta h = \dfrac{v^2}{2g} = \dfrac{gH}{2g} = \dfrac{H}{2}$

$m_1$ rises an additional $\dfrac{H}{2}$ above the point where $m_2$ hit the floor.

Total rise of $m_1$ from start: $H + \dfrac{H}{2} = \dfrac{3H}{2}$

questions.question: An Atwood machine is used in a lab to measure $g$. With $m_1 = 100\ \mathrm{g}$ and $m_2 = 110\ \mathrm{g}$, the heavier mass falls $h = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ in $t = 3.2\ \mathrm{s}$ (starting from rest). Find the experimental value of $g$ and the percentage error compared to $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
questions.answer:
From kinematics: $h = \frac{1}{2}at^2 \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{2h}{t^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 1.0}{(3.2)^2} = \dfrac{2}{10.24} \approx 0.195\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

From Atwood formula: $a = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}$

Solving: $g = \dfrac{a(m_1 + m_2)}{m_2 - m_1} = \dfrac{0.195 \times 0.210}{0.010} = \dfrac{0.04095}{0.010} \approx 9.75\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

Percentage error: $\dfrac{|9.75 - 9.8|}{9.8} \times 100\% \approx 0.51\%$

This is a small error, showing the Atwood machine is an accurate method for measuring $g$.
